prompt: What makes a dashboard panel worth keeping, according to the lesson?

choices.text: It shows as many sources as possible on one chart
choices.why: That is the busy wall the lesson warns about.

choices.text: It updates every few seconds with the newest data the SIEM has received
choices.why: Freshness does not make a panel useful if nobody knows what it asks.

choices.text: It answers a named question
choices.why: Right. A panel whose question nobody can state is one nobody watches.

choices.text: It uses a different colour for each host
choices.why: Colour is presentation, not purpose.

prompt: How many failed SSH logins did the first panel count on Thursday 17, local time?
Why does the lesson ask for a baseline beside every number on a dashboard?

choices.text: Baselines are required by the SIEM to draw a chart
choices.why: The panels in the lesson draw without one.

choices.text: So that the panel can be shown in two time zones
choices.why: Zones are a separate habit.

choices.text: To hide days with little activity
choices.why: A baseline shows them, it does not hide them.

choices.text: A number means nothing without the usual range next to it
choices.why: Right. 70 is alarming next to 8 to 17, and ordinary next to 60 to 80.

prompt: Match each panel of dashboard.sql to what it told the analyst about the week.
What does an alert's severity state, according to the lesson?

choices.text: How confident the rule is that the alert is real, so that noisy rules are marked low
choices.why: That mixes two things; confidence is measured by precision, not severity.

choices.text: Which analyst should take it
choices.why: That is routing.

choices.text: What the alert means if it is true
choices.why: Right. Not how sure the rule is.

choices.text: How many events the rule matched
choices.why: That is the event count.

prompt: A team lowers a noisy rule from high to low so the queue looks calmer. What has it done, in the lesson's terms?
hint: Which field was meant to show the problem?

choices.text: Hidden the problem in the field meant to show it, instead of fixing the rule
choices.why: Right. The honest fix is in the rule's logic.

choices.text: Tuned the rule correctly
choices.why: Tuning changes what the rule matches; this changed only its label.

choices.text: Added a guardrail
choices.why: Guardrails belong to playbooks, lesson 5.

choices.text: Reduced the false positives
choices.why: The same alerts still fire, now sorted lower.

prompt: Why is routing part of the alert, not something added later?

choices.text: Without an owner, nobody is responsible for reading it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Routing deletes duplicates
choices.why: Grouping does that.

choices.text: The severity is computed from the owner's seniority
choices.why: Severity is about meaning.

choices.text: The SIEM refuses to store alerts that have not been given an owner at creation
choices.why: Storage does not depend on routing.

prompt: How many alerts did spray.yml raise, ungrouped, for Thursday's single guessing run?
Why did one guessing run produce 48 alerts?
hint: What happens at each new failure?

choices.text: alerts.sh printed each row twice
choices.why: Each row is a distinct window.

choices.text: The rule is wrong and should be deleted
choices.why: It is right, and noisy; grouping fixes it.

choices.text: 48 different addresses took part
choices.why: All 48 rows name 203.0.113.66.

choices.text: The window was re-evaluated at each failure, and each window over the threshold became an alert
choices.why: Right. Every alert was correct; they all described the same episode.

prompt: Which of these is another name for what grouped.sh does?

choices.text: Deduplication
choices.why: Right. Also called grouping, suppression or throttling.

choices.text: Enrichment
choices.why: Enrichment adds facts; this folds rows.

choices.text: Correlation
choices.why: The correlation produced the 48; grouping folds them.

choices.text: Normalisation, as done by load.py
choices.why: Normalisation names fields; this merges alerts.

prompt: In the sweep, the count drops from 14 addresses at 3 accounts to 1 at 4. What does that drop tell you?
hint: The internet's background noise has a ceiling.

choices.text: That the rule's window is too short
choices.why: The window is a separate choice.

choices.text: That 4 is the threshold every SIEM should use
choices.why: It is this week's measurement, not a universal number.

choices.text: Where background noise ends and the unusual begins
choices.why: Right. Any threshold safely above the drop catches Thursday and nothing else in this week.

choices.text: That 13 addresses were blocked by the playbook
choices.why: The sweep counts flags; nothing was blocked.

prompt: 203.0.113.174 tried 6 accounts over the week, yet the rule at gte 4 did not flag it. Why?

choices.text: It is on the never-block list
choices.why: That list belongs to lesson 5's playbook, and it is not on it.

choices.text: Its failures were for accounts that exist
choices.why: The rule counts accounts, existing or not.

choices.text: Grouping hid it
choices.why: Grouping folds alerts; there was none to fold.

choices.text: In any single hour it tried at most three
choices.why: Right. The window is part of the threshold.

prompt: What should an allowlist entry for a hired scanner carry, according to the lesson?
hint: Two things that keep it honest.

choices.text: A higher severity, so that its alerts appear first in the queue for the whole contract
choices.why: An allowlisted source raises no alerts at all.

choices.text: An owner and an expiry date
choices.why: Right. Otherwise it outlives the contract and blinds the rule.

choices.text: A copy of the rule it bypasses
choices.why: The rule stays where it is.

choices.text: The scanner's password
choices.why: Credentials do not belong in a SIEM's list.

prompt: A rule raised 25 alerts last month and 5 were true. What was its precision, in percent?
What can precision NOT tell you about a rule?

choices.text: How many of its alerts were false
choices.why: That is exactly what precision measures.

choices.text: How it compares with another rule over the same week
choices.why: Lesson 4's two rules were compared that way.

choices.text: Whether the analysts are wasting time on it
choices.why: A low precision says just that.

choices.text: What it missed
choices.why: Right. False negatives are invisible to precision.

prompt: Match each outcome to its description.
hint: Did it fire, and was it right?

pairs.right: the alert fired and it was real
the alert fired and it was not

prompt: Analysts close 60% of alerts from one rule without opening them. What does the lesson say this number shows?

choices.text: That the SIEM is grouping too much
choices.why: Grouping reduces alerts; it does not close them.

choices.text: That the rule's precision is 40%
choices.why: Unopened alerts say nothing about which were true.

choices.text: That fatigue has set in for that rule
choices.why: Right. The rule needs fixing before the one real alert is closed unread.

choices.text: That the analysts are efficient and have learned what is safe to skip
choices.why: That is how the one that mattered gets closed with the rest.
